To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) entrenched CEOs choose lower leverage and shorter maturity, (2) traditional managerial alignment mechanisms have an offsetting impact on the choice of leverage and maturity, (3) founder-CEOs have higher leverage and longer debt maturity, (4) profitability and growth opportunities are associated with lower leverage and longer maturity, and (5) firms with more liquid assets use more long term debt.

1) managerial entrenchment reduces leverage and debt maturity, 2) managerial incentives increase leverage and debt maturity and 3) traditional alignment mechanisms have an offsetting impact on capital structure.
REIT capital structure choices are influenced by managerial entrenchment, managerial incentives, and traditional monitoring mechanisms.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of agency costs and governance mechanisms on the capital structure choice of REITs.
how the capital structure of firms with a unique governance structure (REITs) is influenced by managerial entrenchment, managerial incentives and governance mechanisms.
the role of managerial entrenchment, managerial incentives and governance on capital structure decisions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

managerial incentives and traditional managerial monitoring mechanisms are important determinants of capital structure decisions and that these factors are more important for REITs than for firms in other industries.
the capital structure of REITs is determined by a complex interaction between managerial incentives, governance mechanisms and the firm’s characteristics.
the traditional alignment mechanisms are effective in reducing the agency costs of debt and that entrenchment increases the agency costs of equity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

firms with entrenched managers use less debt, firms with high equity and option ownership use more leverage and firms with high profitability, growth opportunities and liquid assets use less leverage.

firms with entrenched managers choose lower leverage and short maturity debt, firms with high equity and option ownership and high growth opportunities choose lower leverage and shorter maturity and that firms with high liquid assets choose higher leverage and long maturity debt.
managerial entrenchment and incentives influence a firm’s capital structures and that these effects are not offset by other governance mechanisms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
traditional governance variables are an important determinant of capital structure choices, especially in firms where managers are not subject to market discipline.
managerial entrenchment and managerial incentives are important determinants of a firm’s capital structures.
the traditional governance mechanisms that are used to align the interests of shareholders and managers have an offsetting influence on the capital structure decisions of REITs.
